author: Claude (EFL materials writer role), v2 against the quality gate
basis: Rewritten against the v2 quality gate and the grammatical-range check. A2 and B1 were one text with synonyms swapped (vocabulary overlap 0.63, against a ceiling of 0.34 on average), and the B2 climbed by vocabulary rather than by structure, so each slide was re-conceived at each level - the same fact approached from a different angle with different content words - instead of paraphrased down or up. Every fact, name and number of the source is kept (2030 on slide 19 is the mission's only number). Facts corrected, with the reason: slide 3, the workbook B2's 'Margaining either group' is not a word, read as 'marginalising' and written so; slide 7, 'statistics confirm that professional female athletes receive significantly lower remuneration and prize money than male counterparts for identical performance' is overstated as a blanket claim, because several major tournaments now pay equal prize money, so the line keeps the gap but adds that some competitions have moved to equal prizes while the training week is identical; slide 12, 'remaining silent means compliance' is the wrong word (complicity) and a slogan, replaced by the consequence - silence leaves the player to absorb the abuse alone; slide 13, 'finally granting women's tournaments the expansive global audience they rightfully deserve and can monetize' presents an unfinished shift as complete, hedged to competitions beginning to attract serious sponsors; slide 16, 'sports equity directly correlates with robust macroeconomic stability' and 'legal guarantees of inclusion inevitably maximize a nation's complete human capital' hedged to money spent on women's sport tending to repay itself, with the evidence noted as younger than the claim; slide 5, 'stifles cognitive and physical confidence' reduced to confidence in physical strength, which is what the source's own A2 and B1 lines say; slide 9, careers 'cut short' hedged; slide 10, peers 'evaluated solely on merit' de-absolutised; slide 18, the B2's 'ensuring my media consumption reflects compromising equity' is both a typo (presumably 'uncompromising') and unfalsifiable, replaced by a checkable promise - follow one team, pay for the subscription, discuss the fixtures; slide 19, 'build a truly fair sports world by 2030' reframed as the deadline the agenda names and how much closer we can pull it; slide 20, 'Thank you for listening' removed under the house rule that the speech ends on the claim, and 'Let us exit this hall' rewritten. Level is carried by syntax and lexical load, not by word count. B2 earns its level through structure as well as lexis - concession, passive, participle clauses, a cleft, a reduced relative - while staying speakable rather than pompous.

slides.1: Sport is usually filed under entertainment, although it functions as one of the visible arguments a society makes about who is allowed to compete. Today I want to examine gender equality through athletics and the media that sells it.
slides.2: Sport matters politically because it is watched, and what a stadium audience sees on the screen gradually becomes what it believes is normal. Broadcast enough elite female athletes and the assumptions about women's bodies quietly begin to dissolve.
slides.3: The Olympic medal table flatters nations that develop both halves of their population, which is why marginalising either half simply discards talent. Building a balanced squad is cheaper than pretending that only one kind of body can win.
slides.4: Professional competition was reserved for men until very recently, and the reason given was that female bodies would break under serious training. That belief survived for decades, keeping women out of the major international arenas.
slides.5: The lesson is delivered during early childhood, when boys are handed a ball and encouraged outdoors while girls are praised for sitting quietly. Repeatedly described as fragile, girls gradually stop testing their own physical strength.
slides.6: School playgrounds reproduce the same hierarchy, with the football pitch occupied by boys while girls are compressed into the margins. Taught early that the centre is not theirs, many girls conclude that competitive sport was designed for somebody else.
slides.7: Prize money tells the clearest story, because female professionals are paid much less in most competitions, although several tournaments have finally moved to equal purses. The training week, however, is identical.
slides.8: Leadership tells the same story: most head coaches, senior managers and international referees are men. Decisions taken by men alone tend to overlook the injuries, the schedules and the medical needs that only female athletes face.
slides.9: Her second shift begins when the stadium empties, because domestic chores and family expectations still wait at home for the athlete rather than for her male teammate. Unsupported, a promising career frequently ends prematurely.
slides.10: Language is where the culture is actually built, so a phrase like "you play like a girl" should vanish from our touchline vocabulary. Encouraged rather than ridiculed, a beginner keeps returning, and returning is most of the battle.
slides.11: Equal access is easier to organise than equal attitudes, so courts, pitches and equipment should be distributed evenly between the genders. Competing in mixed teams, adolescents rapidly learn to rank each other by ability rather than gender.
slides.12: Sideline abuse and online harassment are challenged far too rarely, which is precisely why they persist. Silence does not keep you neutral, leaving the player to absorb the commentary alone, so intervene while the moment is small.
slides.13: Streaming has rewritten the economics of the game, because a tennis final or a basketball match no longer needs a television network to find its crowd. Watched by millions online, women's competitions are beginning to attract serious sponsors.
slides.14: Sports science has begun to help as well, since wearable trackers now record heart rate, sleep and recovery in detail. Training adjusted around that information tends to prevent injuries rather than repair them afterwards.
slides.15: Social media has handed athletes their own broadcasting rights, and the training footage they publish reaches audiences that no federation ever assembled. Stories written by the women themselves travel further than any official highlight package.
slides.16: Several governments have now rewritten the rules, requiring national teams to be paid the same. Ministers argue that money spent on women's sport repays itself, although that evidence is younger than the enthusiasm.
slides.17: So where does the argument stand? We have traced exclusion, unequal prize money and unpaid work at home, and set against them streaming, wearable data and legislation, which together make athletic equality a plan rather than a slogan.
slides.18: My own commitment is deliberately specific: I will follow one women's team, pay for the subscription and discuss their fixtures like any other sport. I would ask everybody here to choose one comparable habit tonight.
slides.19: Cultural change is slow, and pretending otherwise would insult everyone already doing the work. The agenda names 2030, so the honest question is not whether we arrive on time but how much closer our generation can pull that date.
slides.20: SDG 5 is not a request addressed to somebody else. When the playing field is genuinely level, the competition improves, the audience expands and the record books finally mean what they advertise, and I have already chosen my side.
